opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most exciting consequences of the hierarchical setup. Once you have a robust low-level locomotion policy that takes something like velocity commands or target positions and just reliably executes them over rough terrain, the planner no longer has to reason about joint torques or contact forces. It operates in a much more abstract action space, and that changes what kinds of training are feasible.

For one, you can train the planner in much cheaper simulation. You don't need full rigid-body physics with accurate contacts at every step; you can approximate the robot as something closer to a point or a simple body that moves according to the commands, as long as you have a decent model of what the locomotion policy can actually achieve. That lets you run far more environments in parallel and train over much longer horizons, which is exactly what planning needs.

Second, it opens the door to learning from data that isn't robot data at all. If the interface is "go here" or "move at this velocity," you can imagine using human navigation data, videos, or even pretrained vision-language models to produce those high-level commands. A large model doesn't need to know anything about legs; it just needs to understand the scene and say where to go.

And third, you can mix approaches. Some people use classical planners or search on top, others use reinforcement learning, others imitation. The modularity means you can swap the planner without retraining locomotion, and you can improve locomotion without breaking the planner, as long as the interface stays consistent.

The trade-off, of course, is that you lose some of the end-to-end optimality. The planner might ask for something the legs can't quite do, or miss opportunities that only exist if you reason about the body, like jumping or using a hand to push off. So there's an interesting middle ground in making that interface richer, giving the planner some awareness of the policy's capabilities, without collapsing everything back into one giant network that's hard to train.

r001.rationale: The response mentions human navigation data and videos as possible sources for high-level commands, but does not propose extracting walking trajectories from human videos to train the planner.

r002.rationale: The response lists reinforcement learning and imitation as alternative planner approaches, but does not specifically propose behavior cloning as a replacement for reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing is that once you have a locomotion controller that's robust, that you can trust, the planner doesn't need to know anything about the physics anymore. It just needs to output something like a velocity command, or a target position, or a footstep location, and the low-level policy takes care of actually executing that on the real hardware.

And what that gives you is a much simpler problem at the top. The action space is tiny, the dynamics from the planner's point of view are almost like a point mass or a simple kinematic model, and that means you can train it in environments that are way cheaper than full physics simulation. You can do thousands of environments in parallel with very simple geometry, or even just grids, because you're not simulating contacts and joint torques anymore. So you can explore long horizons, you can train on much more diverse scenes, and the sample complexity drops a lot.

The other thing it opens up is that you don't have to use reinforcement learning for the planner at all. You can use imitation learning from human demonstrations, you can use classical planners to generate data, you can plug in a vision-language model that outputs waypoints. All of those become viable because the interface is so clean. If you tried to do that end to end, with the planner directly producing joint targets, those approaches would really struggle, because the demonstrations wouldn't transfer and the model would have no notion of balance or contact.

And then there's the transfer side. If you train the locomotion policy once with a lot of domain randomization, and it's good, you can swap planners freely, or even swap robots to some extent, as long as they respect the same command interface. So the planner becomes almost platform-agnostic, which is really nice from a research point of view, because you can iterate on the high-level behavior without redoing the low-level work every time.

The caveat is that the abstraction leaks. The planner might ask for things the locomotion policy can't actually do, like a sharp turn at full speed on ice, so you either need to give the planner some sense of the controller's capabilities, or train them with some feedback between the two. That's actually where a lot of the interesting work is right now, in my view.

r002.rationale: It says the planner need not use reinforcement learning and proposes imitation learning from human demonstrations instead, which communicates behavior cloning as an alternative.

astra-6.text:
Once you separate those two, the planner doesn’t need to worry about how to move each joint or maintain balance. It can operate at a higher level, choosing where to go and what velocity to command, while the locomotion controller handles executing that command.

That gives you more flexibility in how you train the planner. You could still use reinforcement learning, but you could also learn from demonstrations, because the demonstrations no longer have to specify the robot’s exact joint motions. They can describe a path or a sequence of navigation decisions.

The important thing is that the planner has some understanding of what the locomotion controller can actually do. Otherwise, it might choose a path that looks reasonable but isn’t physically achievable. So you simplify the problem, but you still need that connection between the two levels.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, so the idea is that once you have a locomotion controller that can reliably execute velocity commands, the planner doesn't have to worry about how to move the legs or maintain balance. It can work at a higher level and decide where the robot should go and what velocity it should use.

And that gives you more flexibility in how you train it. You could use reinforcement learning, but you could also use demonstrations or a more classical planning approach. You can also simplify the simulation for the planner, because you don't necessarily need to simulate every joint and every contact at each step. You still need to capture what the locomotion controller can actually achieve, but separating those two problems makes it much easier to explore different approaches.
